content.text: A good argument has true premises and a conclusion that follows from them. Its premises bear on the issue, and they do not assume the conclusion.

content.definition: Assuming the conclusion in the premises. The argument then goes in a circle.

examples.title: Circular
lines: The Daily Record never prints a false story.
We know because the Daily Record says so.
examples.conclusion: So the Daily Record never prints a false story.
examples.note: The premise counts only if we already trust the paper, so the argument assumes what it tries to prove.

examples.title: A good argument
examples.note: The premises are true, the conclusion follows, and nothing is assumed.

question.prompt: What does it mean to beg the question?
options: To assume the conclusion in the premises
question.hint: Think of an argument that goes in a circle.
question.explanation: An argument begs the question when a premise assumes the conclusion. It cannot persuade anyone who doubts the conclusion.
